name: PulsePoint KneeForge Joint Reinforcement
body_location: bilateral knee — subdermal periarticular, patella and collateral ligament reinforcement with intra-articular sensor nodes
description:
The KneeForge is a bilateral periarticular joint reinforcement system targeting the knee, the single most commonly injured load-bearing joint in physically active workers. The implant consists of a set of ultra-thin woven carbon-fiber and biocompatible elastomer sleeves bonded to the medial and lateral collateral ligaments, the patellar tendon, and the posterior capsule via surgical adhesive and micro-anchor points. These sleeves do not replace the biological tissue — they augment it, providing a secondary load-bearing layer that engages under high stress and protects against hyperextension, valgus collapse, and repetitive-impact microtrauma. Intra-articular pressure sensors embedded in the joint space monitor cartilage stress in real time and relay data to the user's paired health app or onboard PulsePoint display node, providing fatigue warnings before damage accumulates. The system also includes a mild galvanic stimulation component in the quadriceps and hamstring attachment points that promotes faster post-exertion recovery by increasing local blood flow during rest periods.

Delivery runners are the most iconic users of the KneeForge — in GLMZ's vertical geography, a courier running 12-hour shifts across the city's stacked infrastructure levels can accumulate joint stress equivalent to running a marathon daily. But the implant's user base is broad: construction workers on scaffolding, emergency medical responders who spend their shifts standing and sprinting, recreational athletes who train hard enough that chronic knee issues would otherwise end their hobby, and retail workers on hard floors. Many employers in delivery and logistics now include KneeForge installation as a standard onboarding cost because the math is simple — one knee surgery costs more than ten implants. The galvanic recovery function means users often report being able to sustain activity levels that would have sidelined them within a few years, and the joint health data log has become a useful tool for physical therapists and occupational medicine clinics.
installation_requirements: Outpatient orthopedic clinic; local anesthesia; bilateral installation 2–3 hours; 3-week recovery before return to full load-bearing activity
maintenance: Annual joint-stress data review at any PulsePoint clinic or certified sports medicine provider; elastomer sleeves rated for 12-year service life; sensors are wireless-updated

side_effects: Mild joint stiffness and swelling during the 3-week healing period
Some users report a faint clicking sensation during deep knee flexion in the first month as the elastomer sleeve settles
Galvanic stimulation during rest can feel like mild warmth or buzzing in the quadriceps, occasionally disruptive to sleep
Rare cases of over-reliance on fatigue warnings, leading users to push through signals they should heed
cultural_context: The KneeForge is so common among delivery workers and construction crews that its absence is more notable than its presence in those communities. In Tier 1 neighborhoods it is often a first implant — a practical decision made in the early working years to protect a livelihood. Among serious amateur athletes in Tier 2 and 3, it carries a slightly more aspirational flavor, associated with commitment to a sport rather than mere occupational necessity. PulsePoint's marketing leans into both demographics with separate campaign lines, and the brand has successfully positioned KneeForge as neither purely medical nor purely elite — just sensible. There is a small but vocal community of purist athletes who reject it on the grounds of competitive fairness, though no amateur sports body in GLMZ currently bans it.
known_users: Delivery runners and couriers navigating vertical city infrastructure
Retail and hospitality workers on hard surfaces
Physical laborers in Tier 1 who cannot afford injury downtime
story_hooks: A delivery runner's KneeForge joint-stress logs place them at a location they deny ever visiting — at the exact time a corporate courier was murdered there. Someone either spoofed the data or the runner is lying, and the difference matters enormously.

A batch of KneeForge units from a specific manufacturing run are failing at the patellar anchor points, causing spontaneous ligament tears in workers mid-shift. PulsePoint is quietly trying to settle claims before the scale of the defect becomes public.

A competitive free-runner who has become a local legend on the Shelf is approached by a Tier 4 sports promoter — but the contract requires full biometric disclosure including KneeForge logs, which contain evidence of something the runner desperately wants kept private.
